ideas.title: PlaceOrderBatch v2 signing format: EIP-712 `bytes orders` over the canonical packed encoding instead of 400 per-order struct hashes
ideas.area: torus-types eip712.rs (hash_place_order_batch), torus-types lib.rs (canonical encoding), torus-mempool ingest, torus-rpc ingress, tools/bench-throughput signer
ideas.what_needs_to_be_done: Add a new action variant or version, e.g. NativeAction::PlaceOrderBatchV2, or a version byte. Its EIP-712 type is `PlaceOrderBatchV2(bytes orders,uint64 count,uint64 nonce)`, where `orders` is exactly the existing `append_canonical_bytes` encoding of the order list (lib.rs:636-661). EIP-712 hashes a `bytes` field as keccak(bytes), so the struct hash becomes one keccak pass over about 21 KB instead of 400 × (a 2-block typehash plus a 3-block field hash) plus the 12.8 KB concatenation. Put the typehash in a static. Keep v1 accepted for existing clients. Switch the bench generator to v2. Optionally derive `verified_cache_key` as keccak(signing_hash || v || r || s) for v2, so the signing hash and the cache key share one pass. All validators must upgrade together, because this is a consensus and validity change.
ideas.reasoning: Measured cost: in s65-votefix-fix-r1 the follower pool `torus-gossip-verify` burns 7,300-7,750 %CPU·s per load minute. That is 1.22-1.29 cores per follower, 115% usr and 10% sys (threads.log, 04:50-04:53). val0's `torus-ingress-verify` burns the same (1.25-1.29 cores), because the harness sends all RPC to val0. The generator uses 1.45 cores. Per action: 372 CPU·s / 121,366 gossiped actions ≈ 3.07 ms on each follower. The s351 release microbenchmark (memory 6b852ecc) measured the EIP-712 array hash plus ecrecover at about 3.7 µs per order, so a 400-order batch costs about 1.48 ms of struct hash and about 0.2 ms of ecrecover. The struct hash is the largest single component, about 50-70% of the uncontended cost. v2 costs about 21 KB / 248 MB/s (the measured keccak speed on this box, Cargo.toml:63) ≈ 0.085 ms, which saves about 1.4 ms per struct hash. Each action is struct-hashed 4 times on this host: generator sign, val0 RPC verify, val1 gossip verify, val2 gossip verify. 4 × 1.4 ms × ~400 actions/s ≈ 2.2 cores freed, up to about 3.2 cores with the observed contention inflation (3.07/2.1 ≈ 1.46), on an 18-CPU host at load1 33. Calibration: the RATE=270 arms cut submitted actions about 22%, which freed roughly 0.22 × (3 × 1.25 + 1.45) ≈ 1.15 cores of sign and verify CPU. hotstuff runqueue wait fell ~100 → ~80 ms per block and matched/s rose +8.6% (votefix: 59.9k → 65.1k mean of 3), or +8.2% (zerocode r2/r3 vs r270). About half of that gain may come from the smaller backlog rather than CPU. Attributing ~4% per ~1.15 cores and applying diminishing returns to 2.2-3.2 cores gives an estimate of +3-8% matched/s. Unlike RATE=270, it does this without lowering offered load. It also helps the exec-bound late window, where exec runqueue wait is 110-131 ms per block.

ideas.expected_improvement: about 2.2-3.2 cores freed host-wide (follower gossip-verify CPU −45-65%); +3-8% matched/s
ideas.risk: This is a consensus, validity and client-format change, so every validator and the generator must change together. Keep v1 valid. Wallets show `orders` as an opaque bytes blob, which is a UX regression for hardware-wallet users; session-key or programmatic market makers are unaffected. The canonical encoding becomes part of the signing domain and must stay frozen (the test in action_hash_scratch_tests.rs already freezes it). Side benefit: it closes the unsigned stop-trigger hole described in the notes.
ideas.why_new: s64 lists only 'hoist EIP-712 typehashes ... tiny CPU gain' (§5) and 'attest over action hashes' (a proposer-attestation format). No one proposed changing the batch signing domain itself, and no one quantified that follower gossip verify costs 1.25 cores per node, 3.07 ms per action. The planned items A, B and C do not touch per-action verify cost.

ideas.title: Gossip-ingest dedup and digest carry: drop pre-proposal-push re-ingests before the DA re-mirror, and compute the canonical digests once per action
ideas.area: torus-mempool lib.rs add_native_action_from_gossip / admit_gossip / submit_native_action_inner / mirror_to_da; native_pool.rs insert_with_restash_key; torus-state native_da.rs put_batch
ideas.what_needs_to_be_done: (a) At the top of add_native_action_from_gossip, before mirror_to_da, compute the action hash once. If the pool already holds (claimed_sender, action_hash), which means the `seen` set or hash_index hits, return DuplicateNativeAction immediately. Pool membership on this path implies the body was already mirrored, because both gossip entry points mirror before admission (lib.rs:487, :543), so the S459 durable-before-reference rule still holds. (b) Build the canonical preimage once, and derive both `verified_cache_key` (lib.rs:497) and `compute_action_hash` from that buffer. They share `append_canonical_bytes || nonce` and differ only in the signature tail. Pass the cache key into submit_native_action_inner, which today recomputes it at lib.rs:640-644, and pass the action_hash into insert_with_restash_key (native_pool.rs:177). (c) Buffer (hash, wire bytes) in da_pending instead of cloning the SignedNativeAction. put_batch then skips its per-action compute_action_hash and bincode re-serialize (native_da.rs:95-102). The gossip payload already holds the bincode body right after the 20-byte sender (swarm.rs:1352-1356).
ideas.reasoning: The pre-proposal full-body push is routed into the same `native_action_inbound` channel as gossip (swarm.rs:1493-1503). So every body a follower already has is re-ingested: a full ~20 KB DA re-mirror (clone, re-hash, re-serialize, RocksDB put), then two more canonical keccak passes, then a pool Duplicate rejection. val1 logged 329 'received pre-proposal action batch count=200' lines, about 65.8k re-ingests. This matches the unexplained verified_sender cache hits: 142,117 hits minus about 76k exec lookups (383 blocks × 199.6) ≈ 66k. Cost per re-ingest: 3 canonical passes of about 20 KB at 248 MB/s ≈ 0.24 ms, plus the put_batch serialize and hash ≈ 0.1 ms, plus the RocksDB put. About 0.4 ms × 65.8k ≈ 26 CPU·s per follower per cell, and about 1.3 GB of WAL per follower (9% of the 14.4 GB torus_rocksdb_wal_bytes on val1). On the 121k first-time gossip ingests, (b) and (c) save 2 of the 4 canonical passes plus one bincode serialize: about 0.19 ms × 121k ≈ 23 CPU·s. Total ≈ 49 CPU·s / 300 s ≈ 0.16 cores per follower (about 13% of gossip-verify CPU), about 0.05 cores on val0's ingress, and about 1.3 GB less WAL per node. That is small next to the host's ~3 idle cores and 33 load. Scaling the RATE=270 calibration (~4% per ~1.15 cores) to ~0.35 cores gives about +0.5-1.5%.

ideas.risk: Low. The dedup must key on (sender, hash), as the pool does, not on the hash alone, so a forged claimed sender cannot be dropped as 'duplicate' of a real one. It only skips work when the pool already holds the entry, and a committed-and-pruned action falls through to today's path. The raw-bytes DA write must write bytes identical to bincode::serialize(action); a golden test is needed.
ideas.why_new: s64 covers the leader's produce-side re-mirror (#5), commit-side restash and dispatch hashing (#4, and planned C), and a wire-level hash-only push. None of them notices that full-body pushes go back through the follower's gossip-verify and DA-mirror path (66k re-ingests per cell, confirmed by the cache-hit arithmetic), or the duplicated canonical passes inside gossip ingest. This fix is follower-local and needs no protocol change, unlike hash-only push (S387 failure history).

ideas.title: Assigned (sharded) sender verification with QC-certified claimed senders: each action verified by 2f+1 designated validators instead of all n
ideas.area: hotstuff vote path, torus-consensus validate_block / exec sender resolution, CompactBlock format, torus-mempool ingest
ideas.what_needs_to_be_done: 1. Carry the claimed sender per action in the block's hash list (20 B × 200 = 4 KB). 2. Assign each action hash to a deterministic set of 2f+1 validators, for example by rendezvous hashing over the epoch validator set. 3. A validator fully verifies at gossip ingest only its assigned actions. For the rest it admits with verified_locally=false (add_native_action_from_gossip_trusted already exists, lib.rs:529). 4. Before voting, a validator checks that every assigned action in the block is in its verified set with a matching claimed sender. Unknown hashes are fetched and verified, or the node abstains. 5. Exec resolves the sender of every EIP-712 action from the block-carried claim, identically on every node, which keeps exec deterministic. The QC guarantees at least one honest verifier per action: 2f+1 assigned − f excluded from the QC − f Byzantine ≥ 1. Session actions keep full exec-time resolution, because they depend on state. At the devnet's n=3 (quorum 3/3, f=0), each action is verified by 1 node, normally the ingress node.
ideas.reasoning: This is the only BFT-sound way I found to remove per-node verify duplication. The simpler variants fail: seeding the exec trust cache from a validator-attested gossip sender makes sender resolution node-dependent (an execution fork under a Byzantine validator), and leader-only verification with fraud proofs has no enforcement point, because exec is the only guard, the state root is computed but unused, and there is no rollback. Savings at n=3: 2 of 3 verifications per action = 2 × 1.25 cores = 2.5 cores today, or about 0.9 cores after idea 1 (2 × ~0.45). At n=4 (f=1): 1 − 3/4 = 25% of verify work saved. Using the same ~4%-per-1.15-cores calibration: +3-8% standalone, but only +1-3% after idea 1. It also removes the follower's full-verify backlog from the gossip-verify pool, which runs 9 threads per node with 3,400 involuntary context switches/s.
evidence: crates/torus-mempool/src/lib.rs:482-526 (every follower recovers every gossiped sender) and :529-545 (a trusted path already exists, but exec must then re-verify)
crates/torus-consensus/src/app.rs:1646-1662: exec resolves senders through batch_verify_native_actions_cached; a miss means a full recover, so the verification cannot simply be dropped

crates/torus-consensus/src/app.rs:4478-4527: validate_block already trusts a proposer ed25519 sig_attestation instead of re-verifying, so validity is already delegated at validate time and exec is the real guard
crates/torus-network/src/behaviour.rs:85 plus MessageAuthenticity::Signed: gossip authors are cryptographically authenticated validator peers

ideas.expected_improvement: −2.5 cores host-wide at n=3 today (−0.9 after idea 1); +3-8% matched/s standalone, +1-3% on top of idea 1
ideas.risk: High. It changes consensus validity and the block format. The header fast path votes before the body arrives (s64 V1), so a voter must know the block's hash and sender list at header time, and a miss adds vote latency. A Byzantine assigned verifier can withhold votes, a liveness cost that is equivalent to a non-voter. The assignment must be stable across epoch changes. It only pays off if CPU contention stays the limiter after planned item B and idea 1, so do it last.
ideas.why_new: s64 and the planned items never address the n-fold re-verification of gossiped actions. The closest items (exec-verify rayon skip, proposer attestation over hashes) concern exec and validate, not ingest. This design also documents why the tempting variants (trusted-peer trust-cache seeding, leader-only verification with fraud proofs) are unsafe in this architecture.

output.notes:
I read everything from /home/18c/projects/wt/s63-body-fetch (HEAD f05b20e) and the s65-votefix cells. Nothing was modified.

1. Possible security bug, verified in code. The EIP-712 signature does not cover stop-order trigger or limit prices. `append_place_order_fields` (eip712.rs:250-266) encodes `order_type` only as its discriminant (0-3). `StopMarket { trigger }` and `StopLimit { trigger, limit }` values are not in the signed struct for PlaceOrder or PlaceOrderBatch. `grep trigger eip712.rs` finds no hits. The canonical encoding (lib.rs:644-651) and the order book (order_book.rs:422, :458) do use them. So any relayer (RPC node, gossip peer, or leader re-encoding a body) can change a user's stop trigger without invalidating the signature. The action hash changes but the recovered sender does not. Fix: add the trigger and limit to the typed struct, a new typehash and a client change. Idea 1's v2 format closes it for batches automatically.

2. The s64 §5 estimate for 'hoist EIP-712 typehashes' ('tiny CPU gain') is too low. The item typehash string is about 150 bytes, 2 keccak blocks, recomputed for every order. The field buffer is 320 bytes, 3 blocks. So the typehash is 40% of the per-order keccak permutations, about 0.44 ms per 400-order action at 248 MB/s. Each action is hashed 4 times on the bench host (generator, val0 RPC, 2 followers), so hoisting alone is worth about 0.7 cores host-wide. It is a trivial S change with no format change: a static LazyLock<B256> per typehash plus the domain separator. Do it first if idea 1 is judged too invasive.

3. Measured: follower gossip-verify CPU is 1.22-1.29 cores per node in the load window (3.07 ms CPU per gossiped action), about equal to val0's RPC ingress verify. The harness sends all RPC to val0, so val0 publishes 121,366 actions and val1 and val2 each do 121,367 full recovers (cache misses). Exec itself has 0 misses.

4. The 37% of actions that expire are also verified, and DA-written, on both followers: about 45k × 3.07 ms ≈ 138 CPU·s per follower per cell. That waste disappears with planned item B (admission before gossip), so I did not propose lazy or verify-on-select verification as a separate idea. If B's shed is placed after gossip, it should be moved before it.

5. Pre-proposal full-body pushes are re-verified and re-mirrored through the gossip channel. This explains the ~66k 'extra' verified_sender cache hits per node (val1 142,117 hits = ~76k exec + ~66k push re-ingests; 329 pushed batches of 200). This is evidence for idea 2 and for s64's hash-only-push item.

6. WAL bytes on val1 are 14.37 GB against 2.10 GB flushed. Most body bytes are written several times and overwritten in the memtable. This supports the commit-side and produce-side dedup items (planned C, s64 #5).

7. val0 shows ~0.1 core in `torus-gossip-verify` threads during load while torus_native_gossip_received_actions_total is 0. The source is unexplained: possibly push re-ingest from the other leaders (val0 does receive pushes), which fits note 5.

8. At HEAD the pool stores `restash_key` (native_pool.rs:171-230, `insert_with_restash_key`). Part of s64 #4 (commit-side restash recompute) may therefore already be in place. Verify before planning C.

9. Rejected for safety: seeding the exec trust cache from a validator-authenticated gossip claim (makes exec sender resolution node-dependent, an execution fork under a Byzantine peer), and leader-only verification with fraud proofs (no enforcement point: state root unused, no rollback, exec already drops bad-signature actions without slashing per S443).

ideas.title: Apply settle pass-B balance events as one net change per trader: clamped releases add up to min(sum, starting order_margin)
ideas.area: torus-bridge native_executor.rs: compute_market_settle_plan (pass A), settle_market_results_parallel pass B (lines ~4344-4440), BalanceCache
ideas.what_needs_to_be_done: 1) In compute_market_settle_plan (pass A, per market, parallel), stop emitting a per-order `pnl_events: Vec<(&str, Address, FixedPoint)>`. Instead, fold every event into a per-market map (alloy_primitives::map::AddressHashMap) of trader -> {pnl_sum, release_sum, touched}. Taker margin_release, each pnl event (including Some(ZERO)) and each maker/STP release all land here. Use checked_add and return a fallback signal on overflow. 2) Pass B, before any mutation: collect the union of traders and bal_cache.load each one. If any load fails, call the existing settle_market_results_sequential fallback, the same path pass A already uses for fill_error. 3) Then, once per trader: rel = min(sum of release_sum over markets, bal.order_margin); bal.order_margin -= rel; bal.available += rel + sum of pnl_sum; bal_cache.set (this also marks rows that were touched only by zero events, so zero-PnL rows are still written). 4) Leave trade stamping, results and metrics as they are. Optional follow-up with a bigger payoff: the trade index is only a prefix sum over per-market trade counts (base_m = trade_index0 + sum of counts for earlier markets, with no gaps because any fill failure already falls back). Pass A can then stamp final indices and build per-market PackedCfBatches, so trade routing leaves the serial path. 5) Validate with the existing parallel_settle_tests 50x differential (sequential == parallel, byte for byte), plus new cases: clamp-binding legacy state, a trader both maker and taker in several markets, zero-PnL rows.
ideas.reasoning:
Why the result is identical. In pass B a trader's order_margin only ever goes down, through clamped releases rel_i = min(r_i, om) with r_i >= 0. PnL credits touch only `available`. So om_i = max(om_{i-1} - r_i, 0), and by induction om_final = max(om0 - sum(r), 0). Total released is min(sum(r), om0), independent of order, and available_final = av0 + sum(pnl) + that total. So the 'inherently ordered, determinism forbids it' claim in design-parallel-engine.md section 7 is false for the balance part.

Size. s60 pass-B attribution (throughput-campaign-2026-09-18 section 'Accepted pass-B attribution') puts balance apply at 28.2-31.6 ms per invocation, 15-18% of pass B. That is ~59k balance events per invocation (16.0M attempts / 271 invocations), about 0.5 us each. After the change: at most ~5k unique traders x ~0.3-0.5 us, ~2-4 ms, plus the removed per-order pnl_events Vec alloc in pass A and cross-thread free in pass B. Saving: ~25 ms per native block of serial exec.

Today pass B is 85-97 ms/blk early and 150-180 ms/blk in the last 2 minutes (s65-votefix-fix-r1 sampler). In the exec-bound late window the exec chain is ~850-900 ms/blk (engine 683 + save_books ~127 + verify ~42). 25/875 is about 2.9% faster exec, so +3% there, or about +1-1.5% on the 300 s average (late window ~40% of the cell). If the prefix-sum trade stamping is added (trade routing is ~49% of pass B, ~45-90 ms/blk), pass B drops below ~30 ms. That is roughly −60-130 ms/blk late, +7-14% late window, +3-5% average; that part overlaps s64's one-line 'settle pass B parallelization'.

The equivalence rests on (a) nothing in pass B raising order_margin and (b) no balance load errors, which the preload-or-fallback step guarantees. Overflow: aggregated sums use checked_add and fall back to sequential, so the panic behaviour never diverges. The sequential path stays canonical; the differential test gates it. The gain is diluted until the late window is exec-bound.
ideas.why_new: s64 lists only 'Settle pass B parallelization' in one line. The July engine verdict and the 09-18 campaign both treat the clamps as forcing per-event order ('preserve per-trader event order, margin clamps'). Nobody has written down the clamp-commutation identity, which turns the balance work into O(traders) with no ordering constraint, or noted that trade indices are a prefix sum.

ideas.title: Cut per-order work in the Phase-2 margin reserve and the risk caches: one balance load/set per sender batch, integer fast path for the reserve, no position-cache merge
ideas.area: torus-bridge native_executor.rs Phase 2 serial loop (lines 3615-3682), reserve_for_qty_cfg; torus-core position.rs PositionCache; BalanceCache
ideas.what_needs_to_be_done: 1) Phase 2 serial loop: a PlaceOrderBatch expands into a contiguous run of flat entries for one sender. For each run, compute every order's reserve, load the balance once, and if the sum fits in available0 (the common case: orders_rejected_margin_total = 0 in the cell), do one set and pass all orders. Otherwise replay the existing per-order walk on the local balance copy, which has the same semantics. 2) reserve_for_qty_cfg when cfg is None (always true today, see notes): reserve = (p_raw*q_raw)/(SCALE*20) as a single i128 checked_mul and one division. For positive integers, nested truncating division equals division by the product. Fall back to the current `price*qty` then margin_at_integer_leverage path whenever checked_mul overflows, so the panic behaviour is identical. This replaces an ethnum i256 mul + __udivti3 + __divti3 with one __divti3. Reuse it in maker_margin_releases_cfg (2 calls per consumed maker) and exec_cancel_all_run. 3) PositionCache: drop the separate `dirty: HashSet` (keep a dirty flag in the value, as BalanceCache does). In pass B, keep per-market caches in a Vec indexed by market rather than `pos_cache.merge_disjoint`, which rehashes every entry into one map; flush them in market order. 4) Switch BalanceCache, PositionCache and market_batches to alloy_primitives::map (foldhash with a random seed, already a dependency; still HashDoS-resistant). None of these maps is iterated for state writes, since flushes sort. 5) Zero-code probe alongside: TORUS_PARALLEL_ENGINE=4. Its July negative verdict was measured at 400 to 25k orders per block and it was flagged 'revisit for >25k'; blocks now carry ~73k orders.
ideas.reasoning: Phase 2 (exec_phase_margin) is 27-33 ms per native block, serial, over ~73.4k orders: ~400 ns per order. Per order today: 2 SipHash balance ops plus a clone (~60-80 ns), an i256 mul with a 128-bit divide and then an i128 divide by 20 (~60-80 ns), and a SipHash market_batches entry plus Vec growth (~30-50 ns). Folding the balance ops over ~183 sender runs per block, the integer fast path and pre-sized per-market Vecs save ~120-150 ns per order, i.e. 73.4k x 0.13 us ≈ 9-11 ms per block. Removing the position merge saves the measured 5.5-8 ms per invocation of pass-B 'position merge' (s60 table). Total ≈ 15-19 ms of serial exec per block. In the exec-bound late window (~875 ms/blk) that is ~2% there, or +0.5-1% on the 300 s average. It is below the ~9-10% MDE, so validate with phase timers (margin_ns, settle_pass_b_ns) rather than matched/s alone.

The PARALLEL_ENGINE probe adds thread spawns on an oversubscribed host (runqueue 41-48 on 18 CPUs), so it may lose.

ideas.title: Build the missing risk engine on a per-trader snapshot updated from settlement deltas; wiring today's MarginEngine/LiquidationEngine as written would cost seconds per block
ideas.area: torus-core margin.rs (check_initial_margin, cross_margin_equity, total_maintenance_margin), liquidation.rs check_liquidations, native_executor.rs run_liquidation_checks / aggregate_oracle_prices
ideas.what_needs_to_be_done: 1) Recognise the current state: MarginEngine::check_initial_margin / check_margin_at_match, NativeExecutor::run_liquidation_checks and aggregate_oracle_prices have no production caller, and margin_configs is never populated. So open positions carry no margin: a fully filled taker gets its whole reserve back (margin_release = margin_reserved when the order does not rest), and nothing ever liquidates. 2) Before enabling any of these checks, replace the per-call design. Today each call runs positions_for_trader, a prefix iterate_cf through the overlay, three times per trader (check_liquidations, cross_margin_equity, total_maintenance_margin), and run_liquidation_checks repeats that for every market config. Instead, keep a per-trader risk snapshot {balance, positions by market, sum of maintenance, unrealized PnL at the last oracle mark} inside the per-batch caches. Update it from idea 1's per-trader deltas and the pass-A PositionCache. 3) Pre-trade: check free margin against the snapshot, O(1) per order, in the Phase-2 per-sender fold. Liquidation: once per block, only for traders touched this block plus all traders when the oracle moves more than a band, in parallel by trader, instead of all traders x all markets. 4) Wire margin_configs from market listings. Today the listing maps maintenance_margin_bps into 'initial_margin', which never reaches margin_configs.
ideas.reasoning: Zero throughput gain today. This is a safety fix plus avoiding a large future regression. Naive wiring at today's shape: check_initial_margin per order means 73.4k orders x 2 prefix scans (~5-20 us each through the overlay iterate_cf, which merges the DB iterator with two BTreeMap layers and allocates owned Vecs) ≈ 0.7-3 s per block on the serial Phase-2 path. Per-block liquidation over 5k traders x 10 market configs x 3 scans ≈ 150k scans ≈ 0.75-3 s. Either would cut matched/s by more than 50%. The snapshot design costs ~1 us per touched trader (≤5k per block, parallel) plus O(1) per order: <5 ms per block.
evidence: grep: run_liquidation_checks / aggregate_oracle_prices / check_liquidations have no caller outside their definitions (native_executor.rs:5714, 5733; liquidation.rs:72)
MarginEngine::check_initial_margin (margin.rs:91) is called only by check_margin_at_match (margin.rs:164), itself uncalled
margin.rs:179-208: cross_margin_equity and total_maintenance_margin each call positions_for_trader (position.rs:260, prefix iterate_cf)
native_executor.rs:1869 margin_configs = HashMap::new(); no insert anywhere; run_liquidation_checks iterates margin_configs (5742-5746), so it would be a no-op even if called
native_executor.rs:4476-4477: fully filled taker releases its entire reserve; position.rs fill_transition sets isolated_margin ZERO, Cross
native_executor.rs:5556-5562: ListMarket maps maintenance_margin_bps into initial_margin; UpdateMarketParams is 'text-only'
ideas.expected_improvement: 0% today; avoids a >50% matched/s regression when the risk checks are enabled (snapshot costs <5 ms per block vs ~0.7-3 s per block for naive wiring)
ideas.risk: Economic semantics change and consensus-visible: needs a lockstep deploy and oracle availability. Incremental snapshots must be exactly reproducible across validators; recompute from positions when in doubt. Liquidations inside exec also interact with the resident books and the pipelined overlay.
ideas.why_new: Nothing in s64, the planned items or docs/perf covers the risk engine. The s64 margin mentions are only about cancel-all and sender ordering. The dead margin and liquidation path, the unmargined positions, and the O(markets x traders x 3 scans) cost trap are new.

ideas.title: Settle per trader, not per fill event: net balance deltas in pass A, one balance update per trader in pass B, and one balance load/store per sender run in Phase 2
ideas.area: torus-bridge native_executor.rs: compute_market_settle_plan, settle_market_results_parallel pass B, execute_batch_inner Phase 2 serial loop
ideas.what_needs_to_be_done: 1) In compute_market_settle_plan (native_executor.rs ~4446-4560), stop building a Vec<(side, Address, pnl)> pnl_events for each order. Instead fold into a per-market map Address -> (sum_pnl, sum_release): taker margin_release per order, realized-PnL events, and maker_margin_releases_cfg amounts. 2) In pass B (~4300-4420), first pre-load every distinct trader through bal_cache. If any load fails, fall back to the existing canonical sequential path, which already exists and does the same on a worker panic. Then, for each trader in sorted order: rel = min(sum_release, bal.order_margin); order_margin -= rel; available += rel + sum_pnl; set once. Keep the per-order results, trade-index stamping and routing loop unchanged. 3) In the serial Phase-2 reserve loop (~3614-3680), keep the current sender's NativeBalance in a local register while consecutive flat entries share a sender (a PlaceOrderBatch is 400 contiguous same-sender orders). Write it back to bal_cache when the sender changes, instead of a HashMap load, clone and set for every order. 4) Optional: accumulate the per-order Prometheus increments (orders_matched, the funnel counters, self_trade_cancels) in locals and add them once per market. Proof obligations for a differential test against the sequential path: (a) nothing in pass B reads `available` to make a decision. The only clamps are .min(order_margin), and PnL only adds to `available`, so the two fields commute. (b) For non-negative releases a_i against m >= 0, the sequential clamps release exactly min(sum a_i, m) (telescoping). (c) FixedPoint is an i128 with checked add; a pre-sum overflow would panic inside the catch_unwind worker and fall back to sequential, so the outcome is still deterministic.
ideas.reasoning: Balance bookkeeping in pass B is per event, not per account. The s60 TORUS_SETTLE_PASSB_DIAG attribution (throughput-campaign-2026-09-18.md, 'Accepted pass-B attribution') measured balance apply at 28.2-31.6 ms per invocation, with 16,035,318 balance attempts over 271 invocations, about 59k per block. There are at most ~5,000 distinct traders (senders=5000), so at least 12x fewer updates. Estimate: ~30 ms becomes ~3 ms (5k x ~0.5 ms/1k), saving ~25-28 ms. This also removes a per-order Vec allocation that is made on a worker and freed on the exec thread (part of the ~30% 'residual' in that table). Phase 2: margin is 30 ms per block for ~73k orders (26.7M placed / 367 native blocks), ~410 ns per order. Two SipHash lookups plus a clone are ~60-100 ns of that, so ~5-8 ms saved. Total ~30-35 ms per native block on the serial exec thread. Why it pays: val0 per-minute sampler (s65-votefix-ctl-r1) shows exec busy 0.58/0.72/0.81/0.89/0.96 by minute. Minute 5 is exec-bound: exec block sum 57.4 s over ~60 native blocks gives ~957 ms per block, and matched/s fell from 72.0k to 57.5k. -32 ms of 957 is ~3.3% faster exec in the bound tail. Over the 300 s average that is about +0.7-1.5% now. Once planned item C raises the block rate, exec binds for a larger share of the cell and the gain grows toward ~+2-3%.

ideas.title: Exec prologue: hash sort keys only for (category, sender) ties, and stop deep-cloning every action twice
ideas.area: torus-bridge native_executor.rs sort_native_actions / sort_deterministic; torus-consensus app.rs execute_committed_block native section
ideas.what_needs_to_be_done: 1) sort_deterministic (native_executor.rs ~6064-6077) computes keccak256(action.canonical_bytes()) for every action, although the hash only breaks ties between actions with the same (category, sender). Replace it with: stable sort by (category, sender); then, for each run of length >= 2, compute the hashes for that run only and stable-sort the run by hash. The output is identical to today's sort_by on the full key, because sort_by is stable, so equal full keys keep input order in both versions. No consensus change and no lockstep deploy is needed. 2) Remove the two deep clones of all native actions. app.rs:1749 does `sender_actions.push((sender, signed.action.clone()))` inside the replay-guard loop, and sort_native_actions (native_executor.rs ~6032) clones every action again into pre_evm/post_evm. Sort indices or references instead, and let execute_batch take borrowed (Address, &NativeAction) pairs. Its FlatAction already borrows. 3) Add a timer around this prologue, which today sits in the ~48 ms untimed gap of exec_chain.
ideas.reasoning: Per native block, ~185 of the 200 actions are PlaceOrderBatch of 400 orders (26.7M placed / 400 = 66.8k batches out of 72,259 actions processed). The canonical encoding is ~45 B per order, so ~18 KB per batch and ~3.3 MB per block. keccak runs at 248 MB/s on this box (Cargo.toml asm-keccak note), so ~13-14 ms, plus ~2 ms of encoding and Vec regrowth: buffers start at capacity 64 and grow ~9 times per 18 KB. The clones: PlaceOrderParams is ~112-128 B, and ~73k orders give ~9 MB per clone. Two clones plus their frees cost ~4-8 ms. Estimated total -18-22 ms per native block. That fits inside the measured untimed exec gap: exec_chain 715 ms minus (verify 46 + replay 8 + load_books 0.1 + engine 482 + save_books 131) = ~48 ms. Relative to the ~957 ms exec-bound minute-5 chain this is ~2%. That gives +0.4-1% on the 300 s average now and up to ~+2% once exec binds longer after planned C. The tie-only hashing gain depends on selection order. With the old (priority, sender, nonce) SortKey, ~67 low-address senders fill a block and most actions tie, so the gain is mostly the clones. With the arrival-order SortKey now in the working tree (native_pool.rs:13-23, s65 item B), a block draws ~200 of 5,000 senders. That gives ~4 expected same-sender pairs (200^2/(2*5000)), so ~95% of the keccak disappears.

app.rs:1749 sender_actions.push((sender, signed.action.clone())); app.rs:1810 sort_native_actions(&sender_actions); app.rs:1864-1865 execute_batch(&mut ctx, &pre_evm/&post_evm).
s65-votefix-ctl-r1 metrics-after-val0: exec_chain 262.54 s / 367 = 715 ms; verify 46, replay_guard 8.1, engine 482, save_books 131, load_books 0.08 ms per block, leaving ~48 ms untimed.
Cargo.toml:63 'keccak 206 -> 248 MB/s' measured on the 18c box.

Gate it with a property test comparing old and new sort_native_actions on random blocks that include same-sender ties and identical actions. The borrow refactor touches execute_batch's signature, which tests and benches call.

ideas.title: Pass the trust-cache keys that ingress already computed into the exec job, so exec verify stops re-hashing the block body
ideas.area: torus-mempool remove_committed_native / NativePoolEntry.restash_key; app.rs dispatch_to_exec and execute_committed_block; torus-types batch_verify_impl
ideas.what_needs_to_be_done: The working tree (planned item C) now stores restash_key = verified_cache_key in each pool entry at insert. Extend that one step. 1) Have remove_committed_native return the (action_hash -> restash_key) pairs it already reads for the restash. 2) In the commit feed, attach a Vec<Option<B256>> of cache keys, index-aligned with torus_block.native_actions, to the exec job. Use the action hashes planned C already carries into dispatch. 3) Add a batch_verify_native_actions_cached variant that takes these precomputed keys. It uses the key when Some and calls verified_cache_key_with_scratch only when None (actions that were never in this node's pool, or were admitted through the unverified/trusted path, which has no key). The lookup key is byte-for-byte what exec computes today, so hit and miss behaviour, the session exclusion and the 'DO NOT unify keys' rule (mempool lib.rs:143-153) are all unchanged. This is a pure memoization.
ideas.reasoning: With 0 trust-cache misses (verified_sender_cache hits 134,886, misses 0), exec verify still costs 46 ms per native block (16.86 s / 367). Its sequential pre-pass (eip712.rs batch_verify_impl ~1104-1111) recomputes verified_cache_key for all ~200 actions: canonical encoding plus keccak over ~3.3 MB. At 248 MB/s that is ~13-14 ms, plus ~2-3 ms of encoding, so ~15-17 ms per block. The same key was already computed at ingress on this node and stored in the pool entry. Carrying it removes the rehash: -15-17 ms of a 715 ms average chain, or ~1.7% of the ~957 ms exec-bound minute-5 chain. That is +0.3-1% matched/s now and ~+1-2% after planned C. It complements the s64 'skip the rayon phase at 100% hits' item; together they would take exec verify from ~46 ms to a few ms.
evidence: s65-votefix-ctl-r1 metrics-after-val0: torus_exec_verify_seconds_sum 16.86 over count 367; torus_verified_sender_cache_hits_total 134886, misses_total 0.
eip712.rs:1104-1111: the cache pre-pass calls verified_cache_key_with_scratch for every action before any lookup.
torus-types lib.rs:988-1001: the key preimage is canonical_bytes || nonce || v || r || s, a full-body keccak.

torus-mempool native_pool.rs:171-230 (working tree): insert_with_restash_key stores restash_key in NativePoolEntry; mempool lib.rs:989-1003 remove_committed_native reads those keys at commit, before exec.
mempool lib.rs:143-153 and 236-247: the documented reason the key must stay distinct from compute_action_hash is session eligibility, which this memoization preserves.
ideas.expected_improvement: exec verify -15-17 ms per native block; +0.3-1% matched/s now, ~+1-2% after planned C
ideas.risk: Low. The keys are identical bytes, so there is no consensus effect. The main risk is misalignment between keys and actions. Guard with a debug_assert that recomputes and compares a sample, and a unit test that the precomputed-key path equals today's path for mixed hit, miss and session blocks. It depends on planned C's plumbing of hashes into dispatch, so land it in the same change.
ideas.why_new: s64 #4 and planned C store the key so that remove_committed's restash is a lookup, and s64 proposes skipping the rayon phase. Neither removes the exec thread's own recomputation of the cache key for every action in the verify pre-pass, which is ~1/3 of the 46 ms exec verify at 100% hits.

output.notes:
Fees and nonces:
- **No per-action native fees exist.** Phase 4 never touches fees (native_executor.rs:4155). `total_native_fees` is only declared (:1457), zeroed (:1880) and read in distribute_fees (:5801); nothing increments it. There is no per-action fee bookkeeping to batch, and no per-action spam cost either. That is an economics gap, not a perf one.
- **Nonce bookkeeping is cheap and correct as built.**
  - The exec replay guard costs 8.1 ms per native block (exec_replay_guard 2.97 s / 367), and that includes the first deep clone. That is one overlay/RocksDB get and one put per action.
  - CF_NATIVE_NONCES is non-root (backend.rs:1610) but grows without bound (~240 keys/s).
  - Exec does not enforce the 60 s nonce window: batch_verify_impl never checks the nonce. The permanent CF is therefore required for replay safety. An in-memory windowed set would be unsafe without a consensus change that makes exec enforce the window at the block timestamp.
  - Batching the 200 gets as MultiGet might save ~4-6 ms per block, which is low priority.

Smaller findings (not ranked):
1. The per-order `NativeActionResult` vector is thrown away. Each execute_batch allocates n = ~73k entries of 56 B (~4 MB, including `format!` strings on rejects), and app.rs:1864-1865 discards the return value. Cost is ~1-2 ms per block.
2. Redundant hashing at ingress (CPU only, ~0.2 core on val0 and ~0.05-0.1 per follower):
   - The gossip-recover path computes verified_cache_key twice: once in add_native_action_from_gossip and again in submit_native_action_inner.
   - compute_action_hash and bincode::serialized_size run inside the native pool write lock (native_pool.rs insert_with_restash_key).
   - NativeDaStore::put_batch recomputes compute_action_hash for every body. Some of those flushes run on the HotStuff thread through flush_da_mirrors at selection and DA reads, about 1-2 ms per view.
   - The RPC ack does serde_json plus keccak of the whole 400-order action, ~0.3-0.5 ms per action (torus.rs:304-311).
   - One identity hash per action, threaded through all of these, would remove this.
3. rpc_submit_admit_insert averages 3.3 ms per action on val0 (357.3 s / 107,294). This is likely writers waiting on the pool RwLock behind HotStuff's 30 ms read-held restash. It is not throughput-relevant while offered load exceeds capacity, and it does not explain the HotStuff futex time: inserts hold the lock ~100 µs at 357/s, about 3.6% duty.

Evidence that changes estimates:
- The per-minute val0 sampler for s65-votefix-ctl-r1 shows exec busy 0.58/0.72/0.81/0.89/0.96. In minute 5 the exec chain is ~957 ms per block and matched/s drops from 72.0k to 57.5k.
- So the late window really is exec-bound. Once planned item C lifts the block rate, exec becomes the binding constraint for more of the cell, which raises the value of every exec-thread saving above (together ~65-75 ms per block, ~7-8% of the bound-window chain).
- exec_verify stays at 46 ms per block with 0 trust-cache misses. About 15-17 ms of that is the cache-key rehash (idea 3); the rest is presumably the rayon dispatch that s64 already targets.

ideas.title: Build with SSE4.2+PCLMUL (optionally x86-64-v3) so RocksDB uses hardware CRC32C. Today every WAL byte goes through the table-driven software CRC.
ideas.area: build config / torus-state (RocksDB via librocksdb-sys)
ideas.what_needs_to_be_done: 1) In /home/18c/projects/wt/s63-body-fetch/.cargo/config.toml, extend `[target.x86_64-unknown-linux-gnu] rustflags` to ["-C","link-arg=-fuse-ld=mold","-C","target-feature=+sse4.2,+pclmulqdq,+popcnt"]. That is the minimal portable variant: any x86 CPU since about 2010. The broader variant is `-C target-cpu=x86-64-v3 -C target-feature=+pclmulqdq`, which also gives Rust code AVX2, BMI2 and MOVBE and lets RocksDB's XXH3 use AVX2. Use the config file, not the RUSTFLAGS env var. The env var replaces every config rustflags list, including the mold link-arg in both repo and ~/.cargo/config.toml. 2) Rebuild from clean. librocksdb-sys build.rs:117-148 reads CARGO_CFG_TARGET_FEATURE and only then passes -msse4.2/-mpclmul/-mavx2 to gcc. 3) Check the build: the RocksDB LOG must say 'Fast CRC32 supported: Supported on x86'. `nm -C torus-node | grep crc32c_3way` must now be non-empty, and `objdump -d` must show crc32q instructions. 4) Run an A/B of n>=3 matched cells. Watch commit_persist_write, exec_state_write_db, view_duration, CPU per node, and the WAL replay time in a crash cell.
ideas.reasoning: Mechanism, verified: in the s65 node binary (sha256 98116f9f..., the exact binary in s65-votefix artifact-provenance), `nm` shows only `rocksdb::crc32c::ExtendImpl<&DefaultCRC32>` plus table0_-table3_ and no crc32c_3way symbol, and `objdump` finds 0 crc32 instructions. Without __SSE4_2__, DefaultCRC32 (crc32c.cc:251-262) is slicing-by-4 table lookups. Choose_Extend (crc32c.cc:1116) only picks crc32c_3way when __SSE4_2__ and __PCLMUL__ are set at compile time. There is no runtime detection on x86 ('runtime detection no longer supported'). The WAL writer CRCs every payload byte (log_writer.cc:344) and the reader does the same on replay (log_reader.cc:624). Volume: val0 wrote 14.33 GB of WAL in the cell (torus_rocksdb_wal_bytes 41.5 MB before, 14,367 MB after), about 37 MB per native block (383 native blocks). Software slicing-by-4 runs about 2 cycles/byte, ~1.4 GB/s. Hardware 3-way runs about 0.15 c/B, ~18 GB/s. CPU saved = 14.33 GB x (1/1.4 - 1/18) s/GB = 10.2 - 0.8 = about 9.4 s per node per ~300 s cell, about 3% of one core. Critical path: the hotstuff thread writes the ~4.4 MB committed body per native block (commit_persist_write totals 12.2 s over 383 native blocks, ~32 ms each), the leader's ~4 MB mirror and the block insert. That is about 3 ms of software CRC per 4 MB, roughly 6-10 ms per native block, about 5 ms per 620 ms view, ~0.8%. With pipelined writes, the thread that leads a WAL group also CRCs other writers' batches (exec W 4.35 MB/block, trade history, ingress mirrors), so its real share can be higher. The exec writer saves about 3-6 ms of its ~390 ms flush in the exec-bound tail. Recovery: s64 measured single-core CPU-bound WAL replay at ~124 MB/s. CRC at 1.4 GB/s is ~9% of that, so replay gets about 8% faster (~1.5-2 s of a 20-24 s open). The x86-64-v3 variant adds BMI2/AVX2 codegen for all Rust code, typically 0-3% on this kind of code, unmeasured. Total estimate: +0.5-2% matched/s from the CRC alone, up to ~4% with v3, and -3% CPU per node.

ideas.title: Profile-guided optimization (PGO) of torus-node, trained on a matched-bench cell (BOLT later)
ideas.area: build pipeline (all Rust crates; mainly torus-core matching, torus-bridge native_executor, torus-consensus produce/validate, torus-state trie/overlay)
ideas.what_needs_to_be_done: 1) Pin rust-toolchain.toml to `channel = "1.97.0"` (currently the unpinned 'stable') and add the `llvm-tools-preview` component so llvm-profdata matches rustc's LLVM. Only rustc, cargo, clippy, rustfmt and rust-std are installed now. 2) Build an instrumented node: `RUSTFLAGS` via config with `-Cprofile-generate=/path/pgo/%p` (or `cargo pgo build`) into a separate CARGO_TARGET_DIR. 3) Run one normal 300 s matched cell (cap 200, 10 markets) with the instrumented binary on all 3 validators, so leader, follower and exec paths are all covered. %p keeps one .profraw per process. 4) `llvm-profdata merge -o merged.profdata`. 5) Rebuild with `-Cprofile-use=merged.profdata -Cllvm-args=-pgo-warn-missing-function`, ideally together with the already-listed fat LTO / codegen-units=1, since PGO and LTO compound. 6) Run an A/B of n>=3 against the same commit and flags without PGO. Store the .profdata beside the artifact and record rustc and rustflags in artifact-provenance.json. Optional follow-up: llvm-bolt (not installed) on a perf-sampled run of the PGO binary.
ideas.reasoning: The critical path is mostly CPU in branchy Rust code, which is where PGO helps most: better inlining, hot/cold splitting, block layout and branch weights. Typical published results for large Rust services and rustc itself are 5-15% less CPU. Measured CPU on the path: exec_block_seconds 258.0 s over 383 native blocks is 674 ms of exec per native block, the exec thread is ~0.8 busy, and the last ~2 minutes of each cell are exec-bound. Load-window block_build is ~185 ms, on_committed_block ~120 ms and insert_persist (validate) ~170 ms. The hotstuff thread is on CPU ~28-30% of the time, and most of its 70% futex wait is presumably waiting on other CPU-bound threads (exec, peers' validation). Excluded parts: keccak (asm), RocksDB C++ memtable/WAL, and syscalls. Assume ~60% of exec CPU and ~60% of view CPU is PGO-able Rust. Then 8-12% less CPU there gives exec -5-7% (the exec-bound tail gets that directly) and view -3-5% (~20-30 ms of the CPU-bound ~450 ms out of 620 ms). Views/block and timeouts should improve roughly in proportion. Estimate +2-8% matched/s. The low end assumes PGO only trims about 5% of Rust CPU.
evidence: rust-toolchain.toml: channel = "stable" (unpinned); rustc 1.97.0 installed; `rustup component list --installed` has no llvm-tools
Workspace Cargo.toml: no [profile.release]; .cargo/config.toml has no profile-use flags; no PGO/BOLT mention in docs/perf/* or s64 report
s65-votefix-fix-r1 metrics val0: torus_exec_block_seconds_sum 258.04 / 383 native blocks; exec_flush 150.7 s; exec_engine 172.2 s; phase_settle 78.7 s
Task brief: load-window block_build ~185 ms, on_committed_block ~120 ms, insert_persist ~160-180 ms; exec thread busy ~0.8, last ~2 min exec-bound
artifact-provenance.json records commit and build command but not rustc version or rustflags
ideas.expected_improvement: +2-8% matched/s; ~5-10% less exec-thread CPU/block
ideas.risk: The profile must represent the workload. Training on cap-200 order-book load could hurt rare paths (sync, recovery, EVM), but the code stays correct because PGO never changes semantics. The instrumented binary is about 1.5-2x slower in hot loops, so the training cell will have more timeouts. It still covers the right paths, but check that the leader, follower and exec paths all ran. The profile ties to one rustc version, hence the toolchain pin. Stale profiles after large code changes lose benefit; regenerate per campaign. Build time goes up and the pipeline gains a step. Does not cover RocksDB C++; gcc -fprofile-use through CXXFLAGS_librocksdb_sys would be a separate step.
ideas.why_new: The s64 list has 'release profile/LTO' and 'allocator' only. PGO/BOLT appears nowhere in s64, docs/perf or memory. It is a different lever from LTO and stacks on top of it.

ideas.title: Keep panic=unwind and add frame pointers plus line-tables in a bench-prof profile, so the 70% futex wait on hotstuff-algo can be traced to a user-space lock or channel via perf sched_switch callchains
ideas.area: build config / diagnostics (enables attribution for all follow-on work)
ideas.what_needs_to_be_done: 1) Add `[profile.bench-prof] inherits = "release"`, `debug = "line-tables-only"` and `-C force-frame-pointers=yes` (per-profile rustflags need the config-level [target] rustflags or a separate CARGO_TARGET_DIR; keep mold). 2) Do not switch to panic=abort. The unwind .eh_frame tables are what make `--call-graph dwarf` a working fallback today, and catch_unwind containment is used in production code (exec_pipeline.rs, market_workers.rs, native_executor.rs, app.rs, torus-network bridge.rs). 3) On one cell, run `perf sched record -g` (or `perf record -e sched:sched_switch --call-graph fp -t <hotstuff-algo tid>`, falling back to `--call-graph dwarf,16384` on today's binary), then `perf sched timehist -g --tid` to get off-CPU time per user stack. This is a BPF-free off-CPU profile; offcputime-bpfcc was judged unusable in 6843d79. 4) Also record on-CPU `perf record -F 499 -g` for exec and hotstuff-algo. No sampled on-CPU profile exists anywhere in docs/perf or bench-results-matched.
ideas.reasoning: s65 wchan sampling shows hotstuff-algo ~70% in futex_wait_queue, but the kernel wchan cannot say whether that futex is the idle event-channel recv (harmless: waiting on peers) or a Mutex/RwLock held by the exec, RPC or pool threads (fixable). Planned item (A) and s64 items 1, 5 and 10 all assume answers to that question. Rust release builds omit frame pointers, so kernel FP-based user-stack capture at sched_switch breaks at the first Rust frame. Rebuilding with frame pointers (~0-2% cost; bench-only profile) or using dwarf unwinding (possible only because panic=unwind keeps .eh_frame) produces per-stack blocked time. Direct throughput gain is 0%. The value is choosing correctly among ideas estimated at +3-15%.
evidence: git show 6843d79 / docs/perf/blown-cell-diagnosis-2026-09-17.md section 6: offcputime-bpfcc returned zero stacks even for `sleep`; -p mode resolves Rust frames (binary not stripped)
Task brief s65: hotstuff-algo ~70% futex_wait_queue, 28-30% running, <0.5% disk wait (10 Hz /proc wchan)
find over bench-results-matched and docs: no perf report, flamegraph or folded-stack files
catch_unwind in crates/torus-consensus/src/exec_pipeline.rs, crates/torus-bridge/src/market_workers.rs, native_executor.rs, crates/torus-consensus/src/app.rs, crates/torus-network/src/bridge.rs
perf, bpftrace and offcputime-bpfcc installed; perf_event_paranoid = 4 (needs root or a sysctl for the recording run)
ideas.expected_improvement: diagnostic: 0% direct; attributes the ~430 ms/view of hotstuff futex wait to a code site
ideas.risk: Rust's precompiled std may not keep frame pointers, so FP chains can stop inside std's futex/Mutex code. The dwarf fallback avoids this, and at the hotstuff thread's switch rate its cost is acceptable. perf_event_paranoid=4 needs a privileged step. Profiling adds overhead, so do not mix profiled cells into throughput comparisons. Partial overlap with s64 item 9 (wchan/stack sampler): s65 did the kernel wchan half. The user-stack-at-switch half, and the build flags it needs, are the new part.
ideas.why_new: s64 item 9 proposes a wchan/stack sampler and PerfContext timers. s65 implemented only kernel wchan, and off-CPU BPF was declared unusable. Nobody proposed the build-config route (frame pointers, line tables, keep unwind tables) or perf sched_switch/timehist as the BPF-free off-CPU method, and no on-CPU profile exists at all.

output.notes:
Verified facts and side findings:
1) The s65 node binary (sha256 98116f9f..., same as s65-votefix artifact-provenance) contains no hardware CRC32C code. There are 0 crc32 instructions and only the table-driven ExtendImpl<DefaultCRC32>. The devnet RocksDB LOG says 'Fast CRC32 supported: Not supported on x86'. Idea 1 is a one-line config change with an easy build-time check.
2) Other checks, most with nothing to gain:
- Release profile: defaults apply (no [profile.release] anywhere), so debug-assertions and overflow-checks are already off.
- panic=abort should NOT be proposed: catch_unwind containment is load-bearing in exec_pipeline.rs, market_workers.rs, native_executor.rs, app.rs and network bridge.rs.
- Tracing: the steady-state log rate is only ~100 lines/s. About 200k of the 234k val0 log lines are one-time torus_genesis 'seeded genesis account' lines at boot. Compile-time max_level features would not matter. There are 0 debug!/trace! callsites in order_book.rs and native_executor.rs.
- Crypto: curve25519-dalek 4.1.3 already detects AVX2 at runtime, sha2 detects SHA-NI at runtime, and keccak goes through the asm backend. target-cpu does not change any of these.
- The order book uses std SipHash HashMap. The faster-hasher idea is already in s64.
3) Build reproducibility gap: rust-toolchain.toml is unpinned 'stable' (1.97.0 today), and artifact-provenance.json records neither the rustc version nor the effective rustflags. A rustup update between control and treatment cells would silently change codegen. Recommend pinning and recording both. PGO requires the pin anyway.
4) Config trap: both the repo .cargo/config.toml and ~/.cargo/config.toml set target rustflags, which cargo merges. Setting the RUSTFLAGS env var replaces both and drops `-fuse-ld=mold`. Add flags in the repo config.
5) Possible storage finding for another angle: exec_state_write_db averages 161 ms per native block (61.67 s over 383) for a 4.35 MB batch (1.667 GB over 383), about 27 MB/s. That is far slower than CRC or memtable insert of 4 MB can explain, which points to waiting in the pipelined-write group behind other writers or to write throttling. exec_save_books_write adds another 65 ms per block. This is on the exec writer thread, which bounds the tail of each cell.
6) Accounting gap: WAL volume is ~37 MB per native block, but only ~4.4 MB is the exec state batch and ~4.4 MB the committed body. The remaining ~28 MB per block is worth a per-CF breakdown, since duplicate body writes would multiply every per-byte cost, CRC included.

ideas.title: Fix the quadratic Merkle proof build in shard custody, and fuse custody into the body mirror (one serialize, one hash, one write batch)
ideas.area: torus-state erasure.rs / native_da.rs / shard_store.rs (production custody path)
ideas.what_needs_to_be_done: 1) In crates/torus-state/src/erasure.rs, have encode() build merkle_levels once and keep the levels in EncodedBody. EncodedBody::proof(i) and StoredShard::from_encoded_body (shard_store.rs:52) should then slice siblings out of those levels instead of calling merkle_proof(), which recomputes merkle_levels(shards) (every leaf hash) for each index. 2) Change leaf_hash to use the streaming alloy_primitives::Keccak256 (update the tag, the index and the shard) so it stops allocating a Vec and copying each shard before hashing. 3) Replace the separate put_batch + put_shards_batch calls (native_da.rs:87 and :228, called one after the other from mirror_or_drop_native app.rs:4092-4103 and decode_proposal_and_ensure_durable_core app.rs:4262-4282) with one put_batch_with_shards. It would serialize and hash each action once, encode shards from the same buffer, and send body and shard puts in one WriteBatch/db.write. 4) Move StoredShard.shard_bytes into the batch instead of cloning it. Output stays byte-identical: a golden test against legacy_put_shards_batch (native_da.rs:401) already exists as the oracle.
ideas.reasoning: The body set is about 4.1 MB per full block (summary.json dissemination body_push_max_bytes = 4,103,408 in s65-votefix-ctl-r1), or about 20 KB per action. For each action, encode() hashes n leaves for the root, then from_encoded_body calls proof(i) once per index. Each call rebuilds all n leaves, so the leaf-hash total is n + n^2 = n(n+1) per body, over shards of body/k bytes. That is n(n+1)/k body-equivalents of keccak. n=3 (k=2): 6x body = 24.6 MB of keccak per block, plus a 4.1 MB action re-hash in put_shards_batch. n=4 (k=2): 10x = 41 MB. n=21 (k=7): 66x = 270 MB. Keccak on this box is measured at 248 MB/s (Cargo.toml:63; large-input throughput may reach about 500 MB/s). Cost per block per node: n=3 about 57-116 ms, n=4 about 90-180 ms, n=21 about 0.55-1.1 s. The fixed version hashes n leaves once, which is n/k body-equivalents. That is 6.15 MB (12-25 ms) at n=3, 8.2 MB (17-33 ms) at n=4, 12.3 MB (25-50 ms) at n=21. The action re-hash disappears as well. So the fix saves about 50-100 ms per block at n=3-4, and about 0.5-1 s at n=21. The cost lands on the leader's block_build (produce_block, hotstuff thread) and on every follower's insert_persist. View time is about 620 ms and there are about 1.5 views per block. Removing about 75 ms from a production (custody-on) view of about 770 ms gives roughly +10-20% blk/s. At n>=21, custody-on production goes from not viable to viable.

crates/torus-state/src/native_da.rs:243-247 put_shards_batch re-hashes and re-serializes each action right after put_batch (native_da.rs:95-99) did the same
crates/torus-consensus/src/app.rs:4092-4103 (leader) and 4262-4282 / 4339-4353 (followers): custody runs inline after the mirror

ideas.expected_improvement: 0% on today's devnet (custody off). With custody on in production: +10-20% blk/s at n=3-4 (about 50-100 ms/block saved per node), and about 0.5-1 s/block saved at n=21
ideas.risk: Low. The shard bytes, root and proofs must stay byte-identical because the peers' shard-fetch verification depends on them, and the frozen legacy_put_shards_batch oracle test already pins this. Fusing the two writes changes the failure semantics: a shard-encode error must not fail the body mirror, which is fail-closed while custody is best-effort. So encode shards first, and on error fall back to a body-only batch.
ideas.why_new: s64 only says that custody is off in the devnet (item 11, '~20-40 ms estimated') and suggests moving proposer custody to the pre-proposal worker. Neither mentions that proof generation is O(n^2) in the validator count, the duplicate hash and serialize, or that the real cost is about 3-5x the s64 estimate and grows superlinearly with n.

ideas.title: Derive shards on demand at serve time instead of persisting all n shards on every node (drop eager custody from the hot path)
ideas.area: torus-network swarm.rs shard serve + torus-consensus custody call sites + CF_NATIVE_SHARDS
ideas.what_needs_to_be_done: In serve_native_da_shard (crates/torus-network/src/swarm.rs:357), which already runs in spawn_blocking (swarm.rs:1940ff), handle a get_shard miss as follows. Read the whole body from CF_NATIVE_PENDING with store.get_raw(body_hash). Encode it with ErasureParams::for_validator_set(shared.validators.len()) and return shard i with its proof. Keep a small LRU of (body_hash -> EncodedBody or its levels) so the k-1 sibling requests for the same body encode it once. Then make custody_native_shards_core (app.rs:4164) a no-op by default and stop writing CF_NATIVE_SHARDS: every node that holds the whole body can serve any index. This matches the current design assumption in bridge.rs:562-566 that every custodying peer holds all n shards, so peer j is asked for index j. Keep reading already-stored shards for compatibility. Once this lands, the devnet TORUS_SHARD_CUSTODY=0 toggle is identical to production and can be removed from env.sh:56, so bench numbers stop excluding a production cost.
ideas.reasoning: Today every node that custodies writes ALL n shards (native_da.rs:251 loops 0..n) and also keeps the whole body in CF_NATIVE_PENDING. The shards therefore add no availability beyond what the node already stores. They only let a node serve body/k-sized pieces, and those pieces are a deterministic function of (body, k, n) (erasure.rs module doc, 'Determinism'). The serve path is almost never used: native_da_shard_recovered_total, native_da_served_total and native_da_pull_requests_total are 0 on all 3 validators in s65-votefix-ctl-r1, s64-confirm-main-r1 and both s64 crash cells. Eager cost per block per node in production (n=3): the keccak from idea 1 (57-116 ms), RS encode plus bincode plus clones (about 10-15 ms), and a 6.15 MB RocksDB write (1.5x body) in the same WAL and write group as the consensus writes. s64 measured about 45-54 ms for a 4 MB commit-time body write, so about 50-80 ms here. Total about 120-210 ms on the leader's block_build and on each follower's insert_persist. With a view of about 620 ms, custody-on production would run at about 770-830 ms per view, i.e. -19 to -25% blk/s. On-demand serving recovers all of that: +15-30% relative to custody-on production. Serve-side cost is about 0.3 ms per body at 20 KB and only happens on recovery. Storage: CF_NATIVE_SHARDS is never pruned (NativeDaStore::remove only deletes CF_NATIVE_PENDING, native_da.rs:204-209). At 6.15 MB/block x 1.1 blk/s that is about 6.8 MB/s, or about 580 GB/day per node. It would also add about 19% to RocksDB write volume: the measured rate is 12.6 GB over 356 s, about 35 MB/s per node (metrics-after-val0 torus_rocksdb_bytes_written).

ideas.risk: The (k, n) used at serve time comes from the current validator set. Across an epoch change a fetcher might mix shards built under different params. try_reconstruct_from_shards already requires one consistent (erasure_root, k, n, body_len) set and falls back to the whole-body pull, so this can delay recovery but cannot wedge it. The serve CPU cost is bounded by the existing da_serve admission gate. This does NOT deliver Phase-B-style dispersal, where a node holds only its own shard. If that is ever wanted, only the index-i shard should be stored (body/k per node) rather than all n.
ideas.why_new: s64 only suggests moving proposer custody to another thread (production-only). It does not point out that eager custody is redundant with the whole-body store every custodian already keeps, that the followers' custody (on the insert_persist path) is the larger total, or that CF_NATIVE_SHARDS grows without bound. This proposal removes the cost from all nodes and removes the devnet/production divergence.

ideas.title: Make the erasure-shard recovery pre-step end early: count present=false replies and re-check the DA store each tick
ideas.area: torus-consensus app.rs recover_bodies_via_shards + torus-network shard response path
ideas.what_needs_to_be_done: recover_bodies_via_shards (app.rs:2733-2797) sleeps until its deadline unless k verified shards arrive. SHARD_RECOVERY_RETRIES x WORKER_PULL_DELAY = 25 x 20 ms = 500 ms, before the whole-body pull even starts. Changes: (a) have enqueue_native_da_shard (swarm.rs:2932) also record absent replies (present=false) per (body_hash, source), and exit a body's pre-step once (targets - absent) < k; (b) inside the loop, run still.retain(|h| mempool.get_native_da(h).is_none()) each tick, since bodies arriving by push or gossip currently do not end the wait; (c) skip the pre-step entirely when this node has custody disabled, or when the last N pre-steps recovered 0 shards (for example on the devnet, where every node has TORUS_SHARD_CUSTODY=0). With idea 2 in place, (a) mostly matters for peers running older binaries.
ideas.reasoning: Absent shard replies are dropped silently (native_da_shard_response_to_stored returns None, swarm.rs:2911-2914). So with custody off anywhere, every recovery batch waits the full 500 ms, then runs recover_bodies_bounded, which often finds the body already present at its pre-warm check (app.rs:2616-2619). The crash cells show this pattern. s64-crash-combo-r1 has 5 recovery handoffs and s64-crash-combo-off-r1 has 8, both with native_da_pull_requests_total=0. The bodies arrived by other paths while the worker was stuck in the shard wait. The worker is serial, with coalesced batches and a queue cap of 8 (app.rs:2818-2829). A real miss therefore pays 500 ms of dead time plus the 1 s whole-body budget, and later batches wait behind it. Early exit saves up to 0.5 s per recovery cycle. For a rejoining node that needs bodies it can only pull (no gossip replay), that is up to 0.5 s per MissingData re-propose round.
evidence: crates/torus-consensus/src/app.rs:2703-2713 SHARD_RECOVERY_FANOUT=8, SHARD_RECOVERY_RETRIES=WORKER_PULL_RETRIES/2 (25) at a 20 ms delay
app.rs:2765-2796 loop exits only when every body is reconstructed or the deadline passes; no DA-store re-check
crates/torus-network/src/swarm.rs:2911-2936 present=false replies are discarded
crates/torus-node/src/main.rs:616-618 shard fetcher is wired unconditionally, even with TORUS_SHARD_CUSTODY=0
s64-crash-combo-r1 / -off-r1 metrics: recovery_handoffs 5 / 8, pull_requests 0, shard_recovered 0
ideas.expected_improvement: -0.5 s per DA recovery cycle on the devnet and in mixed-version production; about 0-1.5 s off a crash/rejoin freeze depending on the number of cycles
ideas.risk: Very low. It only shortens a best-effort pre-step, and the whole-body fallback is unchanged. Count only authenticated absent replies, so a Byzantine peer cannot force an early exit on its own. Worst case is an immediate whole-body pull, which is the behavior before erasure was added.
ideas.why_new: Not in s64 or the planned items. s64's recovery work covers WAL cap, view-sync and pool-first reconstruction, and none of it touches the shard pre-step's fixed 500 ms wait or the present=false signal being thrown away.

ideas.title: Production-profile bench arm: custody on, 4 validators and WAN shaping on loopback, plus per-node egress accounting
ideas.area: tools/matched-bench run-cell + devnet/wsl env (harness only)
ideas.what_needs_to_be_done: Add a PROFILE=prod arm to tools/matched-bench that: (1) runs with TORUS_SHARD_CUSTODY=1 (the production default, app.rs:176); (2) shapes the P2P UDP ports (30401-30403) on lo with tc (htb rate, e.g. 1 Gbit per node port, plus netem delay of 10-25 ms one way); (3) reports torus_validate_block_custody_seconds, bytes sent per node (read /proc/net/udp or a tc class counter, since gossip_messages_sent also counts direct sends) and header proposal_arrival. Run it n=3 once per release next to the control, so every headline number has a production-gap companion. Use it to validate ideas 1-2 and the hash-only push decision under real egress limits.
ideas.reasoning: The devnet removes three production costs at the same time. (a) Custody: about 120-210 ms per block per node at n=3 by the arithmetic in ideas 1-2. (b) Link bandwidth: every body already reaches every follower by ingress gossip (val0 published 107,294 native actions and val1 and val2 each received exactly 107,294, s65-votefix-ctl-r1). The leader then pushes the full body set again to each of n-1 peers (about 150-160 body_push per node, up to 4.1 MB each), 8.2 MB per block at n=3. At 1 Gbit that is a 66 ms egress burst that can sit in front of the header. At n=21 it is 82 MB, or 656 ms. (c) RTT: the view has about 1 RTT of proposal->vote->QC in its critical path. It costs about 14 ms of header delivery on loopback versus 20-50 ms on a WAN, so +6-35 ms per view. Rough combined production gap at n=3-4: view 620 -> 780-900 ms, i.e. the current 60-65k matched/s could be 20-30% optimistic. The arm is diagnostic. Its value is in not shipping levers whose gains vanish, or reverse, once custody and egress are real. It would likely also move the s64 hash-only-push estimate ('CPU relief only, +0-3%') upward, because the push is fully redundant with gossip here.

s65-votefix-ctl-r1 summary.json dissemination: body_push 153/160/157, body_push_max_bytes 4,103,408
crates/torus-network/src/swarm.rs:2340-2344 fan_native_push sends the full envelope to every validator
no netem/tc support anywhere under tools/ or devnet/ (grep)
ideas.expected_improvement: 0% throughput by itself. It measures an estimated 20-30% gap between devnet and production at n=3-4 and guards the A/B decisions for ideas 1-2 and push/gossip changes
ideas.risk: tc on lo affects every loopback flow, including RPC and metrics scrapes. Filter by the P2P UDP ports only. Shaping is not a real WAN (no loss or jitter by default), so treat results as a lower bound on the gap. Needs root (sudo tc) on the shared host.
ideas.why_new: s64 has no WAN, egress or loopback-honesty item, and only mentions in passing that custody is off. No cell in /home/18c/bench-results-matched has run with custody on, so the production cost has never been measured.

output.notes:
What I found (read-only; code at /home/18c/projects/wt/s63-body-fetch @ f05b20e):

1) The s64 estimate for custody cost is too low. s64 item 11 says custody off 'excludes an estimated ~20-40 ms of production leader cost'. The code implies about 120-210 ms per block per node at n=3, and it lands on followers too (insert_persist), not just the leader. Two causes: (a) proof generation is O(n^2) in the validator count. erasure.rs:220 merkle_proof() rebuilds every leaf hash for each index, and shard_store.rs:52 calls it once per index, giving n(n+1)/k body-equivalents of keccak at 248 MB/s (Cargo.toml:63). (b) Every node writes all n shards (1.5x body at n=3) as well as the whole body. At n=21 the keccak alone is about 270 MB per block, or about 1 s. As written, custody-on production does not scale past small validator sets. No bench cell has ever run with custody on: all cells in /home/18c/bench-results-matched and every devnet/wsl/results report use TORUS_SHARD_CUSTODY=0. One env-only cell (TORUS_SHARD_CUSTODY=1, same build) would settle the number via torus_validate_block_custody_seconds.

2) CF_NATIVE_SHARDS is never pruned. NativeDaStore::remove (native_da.rs:204) only deletes from CF_NATIVE_PENDING, and remove() has no production caller anyway (s64 already notes that). With custody on this is about 6.8 MB/s, or about 580 GB/day per node at the current load.

3) The shard fetcher is wired even when custody is off (torus-node main.rs:616). Absent replies are dropped (swarm.rs:2911), so each DA recovery burns a fixed 500 ms before the whole-body pull. The crash cells show 5 and 8 recovery handoffs with 0 pull requests: the bodies had already arrived while the worker slept.

4) New arithmetic for an existing item: 'hash-only pre-proposal push' (s64 section 5, '+0-3% CPU relief'). Every body already reaches every follower by ingress gossip: val0 published 107,294 native actions and val1 and val2 each received exactly 107,294 (s65-votefix-ctl-r1). The leader still pushes up to 4.1 MB per block to each of the n-1 peers. On loopback that costs nothing. On a 1 Gbit WAN it is a 66 ms (n=3) to 656 ms (n=21) egress burst per block, so the production value of that item is likely well above +0-3%.

5) Interaction with planned item (A), the fast vote-state write: with custody on, a 6 MB shard WriteBatch per block enters the same RocksDB WAL and write group as the consensus writes. Any vote-write speedup measured with custody off may partly disappear in production.

6) Minor: the torus_validate_block_custody_seconds span starts before the enabled check (app.rs:4171-4175). Its count (about 465 per node) therefore counts calls, not custody work. Harmless, but do not read the count as 'custody ran'.

7) The per-action body is about 20 KB (4.1 MB per 200-action block, from body_push_max_bytes). The s46 memory note says about 2 KB per action at cap 25, which is out of date for bs400 PlaceOrderBatch. All the arithmetic above uses 4.1 MB per block. The keccak rate (248 MB/s) was measured on level-hash frames; large-input throughput may be up to about 2x higher, so ranges are given.

ideas.title: Node-role switch: do not build or write trade history on nodes that do not serve it (validators), keep it on RPC/sentry nodes
ideas.area: torus-consensus app.rs exec path + torus-bridge native_executor.rs trade rows + torus-node CLI
ideas.what_needs_to_be_done: Add `--trade-history on|off` (env TORUS_TRADE_HISTORY, default on). When it is off: (1) in app.rs:3262 do not spawn `torus-trade-writer` (trade_writer = None) and do not fall back to the synchronous put at app.rs:2138-2146; (2) add `ctx.record_trades=false` in NativeExecContext so the settle workers skip `TradeKvs::build` (native_executor.rs:4526), pass B skips stamp+route (native_executor.rs:4413-4417), and `persist_trade` (4937) returns early. Nothing else changes, because CF_NATIVE_TRADES and CF_NATIVE_USER_TRADES are outside the consensus root (native_executor.rs:4915-4916, bg_writer.rs:5-10); (3) skip `scan_trades_for_block` in the on_commit_block handler (main.rs:891) and have torus_getTrades/getUserTrades return an explicit 'trade history disabled on this node' error. Bench: run a 3+3 interleaved A/B with the switch off on all three validators (the harness never reads trade history, and the state digests contain no trade rows), plus one arm with it off only on val1 and val2, which are pure validators.
ideas.reasoning: Trade history is the largest non-consensus CPU and IO consumer on this saturated host, and none of the matched/s evidence depends on it. Measured in s65-votefix-fix-r1 over the load window, summed over the 3 nodes: torus-trade-writer uses 0.73-1.47 cores (about 1.2 average); rocksdb:low compaction uses 1.45 → 3.32 cores and ramps up in the exec-bound late window; rocksdb:high flush uses about 0.5-0.78 cores. The trade CFs hold 84%, 100% and 100% of pending compaction bytes on val0, val1 and val2 at cell end, and have the largest memtables (125 MB each on val1). WAL arithmetic: 22.44M fills × (297 B payload + about 12 B WriteBatch framing) = 6.9 GB of the 14.33 GB WAL delta per node, so about 48% of all WAL bytes. Trade-attributable CPU ≈ 1.2 (writer) + 60-85% × 2.45 (compaction) + about 50% × 0.65 (flush) ≈ 2.9-3.6 cores out of 18, i.e. 16-20% of the host. vmstat shows the host at 1-6% idle with run queue 35-60 in the load window. hotstuff-algo is runnable-but-waiting about 11% of wall time (pidstat %wait 31-38 summed over 3 nodes), and flush-worker about 13%. Freeing about 3 cores should roughly halve that runqueue wait on the critical threads, worth about -35-45 ms of a ~650-860 ms chain step (4-5%). Compaction CPU peaks in the exec-bound last ~2 minutes, so the late window gains too. Discounted for elastic pools (gossip-verify, rayon) absorbing some of the freed CPU: +3-8% with all nodes off, about 2/3 of that with val1/val2 only. Precedent: Hyperliquid's hl-node writes fills and trades only behind opt-in flags.

ideas.expected_improvement: +3-8% matched/s with all validators off (+2-5% with only val1/val2 off); frees about 3 host cores and halves WAL bytes
ideas.risk: Low for consensus, since the rows are outside the root. It is a product decision: a node with the switch off cannot answer trade-history RPCs, so the RPC/explorer nodes must keep it on, and WS new_trades is empty on those nodes. Report the result as a separate operating point ('validator without history'), not as a like-for-like record.
ideas.why_new: s64 has only 'trade writer: disable_wal and drop low_pri' and a consensus-KV split. Neither removes the work. No doc proposes a validator/RPC role split for trade history, and none quantifies its host CPU (about 3 cores, 16-20%) or its WAL share (48%).

ideas.title: The cosmetic trade writer must never backpressure exec: byte-bounded, non-blocking hand-off with drop-and-count on overflow
ideas.area: torus-state bg_writer.rs + app.rs trade hand-off
ideas.what_needs_to_be_done: In BackgroundCfWriter, add a lossy mode that only the trade writer uses: `send_packed` uses `try_send`. The bound is in queued BYTES (e.g. 512 MB via TORUS_TRADE_WRITER_MAX_MB), not the current 256 batches. On Full, drop the batch, increment `torus_trade_writer_dropped_batches_total`, and record the dropped height range in a small node-local marker, so RPC can report a history gap instead of silently missing rows. Keep the blocking behaviour for `post_flush_writer`, which carries recovery-relevant body rows. Also pre-size the per-block `PackedCfBatch` from the previous block's len/rows (native_executor.rs:1883 uses Default, so it grows by doubling on the exec thread). Export queued bytes as a gauge; today `trade_writer_queued_batches` only updates on send and freezes when load stops.
ideas.reasoning: The writer already falls behind at today's rate. The queue grows from 9 to 102 batches between t=183 and t=334 s in s65-votefix-ctl-r2 (0.62 batches/s) and ends at 50-102 in every s65 cell. Its jumps line up with `l0_files_max`=8 samples (ctl-r2 t≈198-213: 19→37; fix-r1 t≈345-365: 7→21→34). That fits RocksDB's DB-wide compaction-speedup condition, which throttles low_pri writes to the 1 MB/s low-pri limiter. At 0.34-0.62 batches/s the 256-batch cap is reached at about t≈580-900 s. After that `tx.send` blocks the exec thread (app.rs:3260-3261 says so), so exec runs at the writer's drain rate, about 1.14-0.62 ≈ 0.5-0.8 native blk/s against 1.14 today: −30-55% matched/s in any run longer than ~10-15 minutes. Memory: each queued batch is 58.6k fills × 297 B = 17.4 MB of arena plus 175.8k × 40 B = 7 MB of row index, about 24 MB resident. 55-102 queued batches is therefore 1.3-2.5 GB of RSS per node at 300 s (a large part of the 7.7 GB RSS in s64). At the 256 cap it is about 6 GB, which exceeds the documented 8 GB validator class once the 1.25 GB DB budget is added. The older s60 600 s cell (exec-bound at 34k fills/s) kept the queue at about 1. The cliff appeared only at today's ~60k+ fills/s.
